<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README content, here’s how to approach drawing a detailed, accurate system design diagram for the “Tech Interview Handbook” project.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • The repository is organized as a monorepo containing multiple “apps” and “packages.” The main public-facing components are the “portal” app (in apps/portal) and the “website” (in apps/website). The portal app is a Next.js application with a strong backend component (using API routes, tRPC routers, NextAuth for authentication, and Prisma for database interactions), while the website is built with Docusaurus (or a similar static site generator) to serve curated interview content, blog articles, and supplementary materials.
   • The general purpose is to deliver curated technical interview preparation content along with interactive tools (for resumes, coding interview study plans, and question contributions) and a supporting community around interview preparation.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   • There are obvious separations for the different applications:
     - apps/portal: Contains Next.js application files including pages, components, API routes, server routers, Prisma schemas and migrations, environment configuration files (.env.example), and styling assets. This app likely represents the interactive “portal” where users can log in, submit offers, view resumes, and interact with curated interview materials.
     - apps/website: Contains a Docusaurus site (or similar) with blog posts, static content, and additional pages. It serves as a public-facing website that provides the curated handbook content.
     - packages: Contains shared configuration such as ESLint, Tailwind settings, and TypeScript configurations targeted at standardizing the development environment across the monorepo.
     - algorithms: Possibly a repository of algorithm-related readmes and utilities.
   • The presence of a turborepo configuration (turbo.json) and pnpm workspace files indicate that the project is managed as a monorepo and may benefit from a layered architecture (sharing common packages and utilities across apps).

3. Components & Their Relationships:
   • Frontend (Browser/Client):
     - Two entry points: one for the “portal” Next.js app and one for the “website.” They are separate clients but may share common design assets via packages.
     - In the portal, client-side views interact with components (found under apps/portal/src/components) that offer a range of functionality (offers, questions, resumes, etc.).
   • Backend/API:
     - The portal app has API routes (found under apps/portal/src/pages/api) including authentication (using NextAuth), tRPC endpoints, and a set of REST-like routers for domains such as companies, questions, resumes, todos, etc.
     - The server logic and database interactions are implemented with Prisma (found in apps/portal/prisma/), which manages schema definitions, migrations, and seeding.
   • Database:
     - The Prisma schema file and numerous migrations indicate a relational database is in use (the specifics aren’t in the tree, but it is managed through Prisma).
   • Shared Code and Configurations:
     - Packages for ESLint, Tailwind, and TypeScript exist in the “packages” directory, indicating these are shared toolsets across the apps.
     - Common utilities and shared components (e.g., the “shared” UI components and utilities in apps/portal/src/ui and apps/portal/src/utils) provide consistency in coding patterns.
   • External Services & Integrations:
     - Authentication is likely handled via NextAuth.
     - There are modules for Google Analytics embedded in the global components.
     - The use of environment configuration files (.env.example) suggests integration with external APIs or services where credentials are managed.
     - The README links to external interview preparation courses and communities, which although external, provide contextual direction for the service.

4. Architectural Patterns and Design:
   • Monorepo structure using pnpm-workspace and Turborepo implies a modular and scalable design where changes in shared packages affect both apps.
   • In the portal, a typical Next.js full-stack pattern is present where client code, server routes, and API endpoints coexist. The routing is done based on file paths (pages directory) and is further modularized through the use of tRPC routers.
   • The separation between rendering (pages, components) and service logic (routers, database access) adheres to best practices for full-stack Next.js applications.
   • The website content is rendered statically (using Docusaurus or similar) which follows a “content as code” methodology.

5. Guidelines for Creating the System Design Diagram:
   a. Identify and label the main components:
      • Portal App:
          - Client (Browser) → renders Next.js UI (apps/portal/src/components)
          - API layer (Next.js API routes, tRPC endpoints in apps/portal/src/pages/api and apps/portal/src/server/router)
          - Authentication (NextAuth via API routes)
          - Business Logic and Utilities (server folder, mappers, and various utility functions)
          - Database (Prisma schema, migrations in apps/portal/prisma)
      • Website:
          - Static content rendering (Docusaurus website found under apps/website)
          - Blog, Documentation, and Interactive Content Pages
      • Shared/Configuration Packages:
          - ESLint, Tailwind, TypeScript configurations (in packages/)
      • External Integrations:
          - Analytics (Google Analytics module)
          - External authentication providers (per NextAuth configuration)
          - Possibly third-party interview/coding course links and affiliates (as noted in README)
   
   b. Draw Relationships and Interactions:
      • Use directional arrows to denote data flow:
          - From the Client (Portal) to the API layer, showing calls to authenticated endpoints.
          - The API layer accessing and manipulating data in the Database.
          - Shared packages providing common configuration to both apps.
          - The Website’s static content pulls in design assets/resources, and may link externally to the portal.
      • Clearly show dependencies between the client UI components, API server components, and the database.
   
   c. Highlight Architectural Patterns:
      • Monorepo structure with two distinct apps (portal and website) alongside shared configuration packages.
      • Next.js full-stack app pattern in the portal where server and client code are closely integrated.
      • Separation of content delivery (static website) and interactive application (portal) components.
   
   d. Include Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
      • Next.js for the portal UI and API routes.
      • TypeScript for static type checking.
      • Prisma for database access and migrations.
      • NextAuth (and potentially tRPC) for authentication and API communication.
      • Docusaurus (or similar) for static content and documentation in the website.
      • Tailwind CSS for styling (shared across apps through packages/tailwind-config).
      • ESLint and Prettier for code quality and formatting.
      
6. Tailoring the Diagram to the Specific Project:
   • Since this is a full-stack application with a static website component, ensure you clearly separate the interactive portal from the content website.
   • Within the portal, break down the architecture to show the client-side application, the API/server layer, and the database layer.
   • Make sure to incorporate the shared packages that are used throughout the monorepo, as these are vital to the uniform configuration across different parts of the project.
   • In the diagram, denote external dependencies (for example, third-party authentication providers or analytics services) to give a holistic view of all integrations.
   
7. Diagram Details and Presentation:
   • Use clear labels for each component, such as “Client (Portal UI)”, “API Gateway / tRPC Routes”, “Database (Prisma Managed)”, “Static Website (Docusaurus)”, and “Shared Config Packages.”
   • Draw directional arrows to show data flow:
          - Arrow from the “Client” to “API Layer” (showing API requests).
          - Arrow from “API Layer” to “Database” (showing data queries and mutations).
          - Arrows from “Client” to “External Services” (for analytics and authentication).
          - Indicate the flow of static content from the build process of the website.
   • Consider using different shapes (rectangles for applications, cylinders for databases, cloud icons for external services) and color coding (one color per app or area) to enhance readability.
   • Keep the diagram detailed but organized—don’t overcomplicate it, but ensure all essential components and interconnections are captured.

By following these guidelines, you will create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the modular, full-stack, and multi-application nature of the Tech Interview Handbook project. This will be a useful reference for understanding component responsibilities, data flows, and technology integrations within the monorepo.
</explanation>
